Re-read all cited code in the current codebase and the claim holds exactly.

Frontend src/components/superadmin/SAParents.js:
- Line 17: `const DEFAULT_PW = 'Parent@123';` — confirmed byte-for-byte.
- Line 134: `password: d.password || form.password || DEFAULT_PW,` — confirmed. The credentials modal's password field uses this fallback chain when building `setCreds(...)` after a successful POST to /api/parents/.

Backend: /api/parents/ POST routes to data.createSuperParent (src/routes/superadmin.js:278). In src/controllers/superadminDataController.js:
- Line 3282: `const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(data.password || 'Parent@123', 10);` — confirmed, the backend independently hardcodes the identical literal 'Parent@123'.
- Line 3309: `return res.json(successResponse({ id: parent.id, user_id: user.id, username }, 'Parent created'));` — the response contains id, user_id, username but NOT password. successResponse spreads data at top level (authController-style `{ success, message, ...data }`), so d.username works, but d.password is always undefined.

Consequence: because the API never returns a password, the `d.password ||` branch in line 134 is effectively dead — the modal ALWAYS resolves to `form.password || DEFAULT_PW`. When the admin leaves the password blank, the modal shows the frontend constant 'Parent@123' while the backend hashes its own independent 'Parent@123'. They are equal today, so the displayed password is correct. But the two literals are duplicated and uncoupled; if a backend dev changes the default in createSuperParent without updating SAParents.js:17, the modal would display a password that doesn't match the stored hash and parents would be locked out with no error surfaced. The ironic part is the in-code comment at lines 132-133 ("Prefer the server-generated password so the admin copies the REAL one") describes a behavior that does not happen, since the endpoint omits the password.

Severity low is appropriate: no current user impact (values match), no security hole (just a duplicated default literal), but it is a genuine latent maintainability/UX footgun. The suggested fix (have createSuperParent return the effective generated password instead of relying on a duplicated literal) is correct.

Reproduced every cited fact in the current codebase. principal.js:15-18 applies ONLY `router.use(authenticateToken)` and `router.use(schoolScope)` — no requireRole anywhere in the file (entire router re-read, lines 1-38). auth.js:6-46 only verifies the JWT and sets req.user (plus a best-effort impersonation audit log on mutating methods); it performs no role check. schoolScope.js:1-11 only pins req.schoolId from the caller's school_id (or ?school_id for superadmins) — no role restriction. principal.js:33 wires `router.get('/attendance-report/', getAttendanceReport)`, mounted at index.js:142 (`app.use('/api/principal', principalRouter)`). getAttendanceReport (principalController.js:442-495) calls getSchoolFromUser(req), which (lines 19-28) resolves the school as `req.schoolId || req.user.school_id` — i.e. the caller's OWN JWT — then aggregates Attendance where school_id = that school and returns school-wide present/absent/late/excused counts per class plus overall rate and low-attendance count. So any authenticated user in the school (student, parent, teacher, bursar) can curl GET /api/principal/attendance-report/ with their own token and receive principal-level analytics. The contrast in the finding also holds: requireRole IS used on sibling routers — finance.js:55/57, school.js:152, superadmin.js:112/227. No cross-tenant leak (school is pinned to the caller's own school), but it is a genuine cross-role information disclosure within the tenant. Severity medium is appropriate: read-only, intra-tenant, non-PII aggregate analytics, but exposed to roles the UI never grants it to. Note: the same missing gate applies to the entire /api/principal/* router (overview, class-performance, teacher-insights, finance-snapshot, syllabus-progress, grade-approvals, report-cards, principal-users including POST/PUT mutations) — the finding scopes to attendance-report but the authorization gap is router-wide, which arguably makes the broader exposure worse than this single endpoint.
